summary.title: Learning Rust With Entirely Too Many Linked Lists
summary.one_liner: You learn intermediate and advanced Rust (ownership, Box, Rc, raw pointers, unsafe) by implementing six different linked lists, while getting a critical view of when linked lists are actually worth using.
keywords: learn rust by building data structures
box rc arc pointers in rust
takeaways: Build six linked lists (stacks, deques, a queue, and persistent lists) to learn Rust concepts progressively.
Covers pointer types such as &, &mut, Box, Rc, Arc, *const, *mut and NonNull, plus ownership and interior mutability.
Introduces unsafe Rust topics: raw pointers, aliasing, stacked borrows, UnsafeCell and variance, with miri for testing.
The author argues that Vec or VecDeque is usually the better choice and lists the rare cases where linked lists fit.
summary.summary: This is an online book that teaches Rust by having the reader implement six linked lists, from a basic singly-linked stack to an unsafe queue and a persistent list, with a bonus chapter of other lists. It is written against Rust 2018 and uses cargo for the project, rustup for toolchains, and miri for checking unsafe code. The tone is informal and deliberately shows compiler errors as part of learning. Its preface also contains a long argument that linked lists are niche and that Vec or VecDeque is usually the better choice, with the performance and memory trade-offs explained.
